back: O(n!) — full permutation generation, brute-force backtracking.
O(2^n) — subsets, bitmask DP.
O(n^3)-O(n^4) — 2-D / interval DP, Floyd-Warshall.
O(n^3) — interval DP.
O(n^2) — nested loops, 2-D DP.

front: Answer space is huge but MONOTONIC (if X works, X+1 works)
back: Binary search on the answer. Write a Feasible(x) predicate, then binary search the smallest feasible x.

front: Find two numbers summing to target, array UNSORTED
back: Hash map value -> index, single pass. Check for the complement BEFORE inserting the current element.

front: Find a pair summing to target, array IS SORTED
back: Two pointers from opposite ends. Sum too small -> lo++. Too big -> hi--.
Variable-size sliding window + frequency map. Expand right every iteration; while-shrink from left until valid.
Fixed-size sliding window. Add nums[right], remove nums[right-k].
Variable sliding window + Dictionary count. Shrink while count.Count > k.
Prefix sum + hash map of prefix-sum counts. Answer += map[running - k]. Seed map[0] = 1.
Character frequency map, or an int[26] array. Compare counts, don't sort (sorting is O(n log n)).

front: Detect a cycle in a linked list
back: Fast/slow pointers (Floyd). fast moves 2, slow moves 1; they meet iff there's a cycle.

front: Find the middle of a linked list in ONE pass
back: Fast/slow pointers. When fast hits the end, slow is at the middle.

front: Reverse a linked list or a sublist
back: Three-pointer dance: prev / cur / next. Use a dummy node if the head can change.
Dummy node + tail pointer + two pointers. Finish with tail.next = a ?? b.
Monotonic DECREASING stack holding indices. Pop while the new value is greater.
Monotonic stack (histogram), or two pointers tracking running max from each side (rain water).
Stack. Push openers, pop and match on closers, require empty at the end.
Heap of size k (or quickselect for O(n) average). Watch the heap direction — see the 'which heap' card.
Two heaps: max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half. Rebalance so sizes differ by at most 1.
Min-heap holding the current head of each of the k lists. O(N log k).
Modified binary search: one half is always sorted — determine which, then decide if the target lies inside it.
Binary search on the answer space + a greedy Feasible(x) check.

front: 'Ship packages in D days' / 'Koko eating bananas' / 'split array'
back: Binary search on the answer + a greedy feasibility simulation. Classic disguise for binary search.
Sort by START, then sweep merging while cur.start <= last.end.
Min-heap of end times; OR sweep line with +1 on start / -1 on end and track the running max.
Sort by END, greedily take each interval that starts after the last taken one ends.

front: 'Number of islands' / connected regions in a grid
back: BFS or DFS flood fill. Mark visited IN PLACE to avoid a separate visited set.

front: 'Shortest path' in an UNWEIGHTED graph or grid
back: BFS. Never DFS — DFS does not yield shortest paths.
Multi-source BFS: enqueue ALL sources at level 0, then count levels.
Topological sort via Kahn's algorithm (in-degree + queue). Leftover nodes means a cycle.

front: Detect a cycle in a DIRECTED graph
back: DFS with 3 colours (unvisited / in-stack / done), or Kahn's — if the topo order is shorter than n, there's a cycle.
Union-Find (disjoint set) with path compression.
Dijkstra: min-heap keyed by distance. (Negative weights -> Bellman-Ford.)
Backtracking: choose -> recurse -> UN-choose. Add a COPY of the path to results.
Backtracking DFS from every cell, marking the cell in place and restoring it on the way out.
Backtracking tracking open and close counts. Add '(' if open < n; add ')' if close < open.
Trie. Node with Node[26] children + a bool end-of-word flag.

front: 'Number of ways to reach step n'
back: 1-D DP with a Fibonacci-shaped recurrence: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2].

front: 'Minimum cost / maximum profit to reach the end'
back: 1-D DP. Define dp[i] = best value considering the first i items, then find the recurrence.
House-robber 1-D DP: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]).
Unbounded knapsack DP. Inner loop runs FORWARD so an item can be reused.
O(n^2) DP, or O(n log n) patience sorting with binary search over tail values.

front: Two strings compared (edit distance, LCS, interleaving)
back: 2-D DP table of size (m+1) x (n+1). Row 0 / column 0 are the base cases.

front: 'Unique paths' / 'minimum path sum' in a grid
back: 2-D DP over the grid; often compressible to a 1-D rolling row.
Dictionary (key -> node) + doubly linked list for recency. Both operations O(1).
Auxiliary stack storing the running minimum, pushed in lockstep with the main stack.
DFS carrying (min, max) bounds downward. Comparing only parent to child is WRONG.
In-order traversal yields sorted order; count nodes as you go and stop at k.
General tree: DFS returning the node when left and right both return non-null. BST: walk down while both values are on the same side.
BFS with a level-size loop: capture q.Count before the inner for-loop.
Pre-order DFS with explicit null markers; deserialize by consuming the same stream in the same order.
Spiral: four boundary pointers shrinking inward. Rotate: transpose, then reverse each row.
Use the first row and first column as marker storage; handle those two separately with flags.

front: 'Find the duplicate without modifying the array, O(1) space'
back: Floyd cycle detection treating values as next-indices.

front: 'Majority element appearing more than n/2 times'
back: Boyer-Moore voting: keep a candidate and a count.
Prefix products pass, then suffix products pass, multiplied together.

front: Problem demands 'O(1) extra space' on an array
back: In-place marking (negate values / swap to index), index-as-hash, or two pointers.
Two pointers from both ends moving inward.

front: Backtracking: adding the current path to the results
back:
Add a COPY: res.Add(new List<int>(path));
Adding the reference means every result aliases the same list, which ends up empty.

Carry (min, max) bounds DOWN the recursion.
Comparing only parent to child is wrong — a deep descendant can still violate the BST property.

front: BFS or DFS for shortest path?
back:
BFS. DFS does NOT produce shortest paths in an unweighted graph.
Weighted edges -> Dijkstra instead.

front: When do I need a dummy node on a linked list?
back:
Whenever the HEAD might change: deleting the head, inserting before it, or merging lists.
It removes the special case entirely.

while (lo < hi) with hi = mid / lo = mid + 1 is SAFE.
while (lo <= hi) combined with hi = mid loops forever. Pick one template and never improvise.

front: Grid DFS/BFS: when to mark a cell visited
back:
Mark it BEFORE recursing or when enqueueing — never after.
Marking late lets the same cell enter the queue many times.

front: Sliding window: what shrinks and what advances
back:
right advances exactly once per outer iteration.
The inner WHILE shrinks from the left until the window is valid again. Never shrink with an if.

front: Two-sum hash map: check or insert first?
back:
CHECK for the complement BEFORE inserting the current element.
Otherwise an element matches itself when target == 2 * nums[i].

10^5 elements of magnitude 10^9 overflow int when summed. Use long.
Also watch mid-point arithmetic and products.

A skewed tree or 10^5-node linked list will stack overflow.
If constraints say n is around 10^5 and recursion is linear-depth, convert to iterative.

k LARGEST -> MIN-heap of size k (evict the smallest).

Memorise this; it is backwards from intuition.

front: DP: direction of the inner loop
back:
0/1 knapsack (each item once) -> iterate capacity BACKWARD.
Unbounded knapsack (reuse items) -> iterate capacity FORWARD.
Generally: dp[i] may only read already-finalised cells.

front: Modifying a collection while iterating it
back:
Throws InvalidOperationException in C#.
Collect the keys first (d.Keys.ToList()) and iterate that copy.

Never stay silent for more than ~20 seconds.
Interviewers are instructed to hint, but can only hint on an idea you have stated out loud.
A wrong idea spoken beats silence every time.

front: Interview behaviour: before writing any code
back:
State the pattern, the insight and the target complexity, then ask:
'Does this approach sound reasonable before I code it?'
This buy-in step is a senior-level signal and prevents 20 wasted lines.
